criteria.note: The exact keyword intent — Korean phrases for gluten-free dining — is served inside the first 100 words with the hero sentence in Hangul plus English gloss, and the framing decision (allergy over 'gluten-free') follows immediately.
Title with the appended site suffix is ~50 chars, description ~135 chars, keyword tokens present in both, and neither restates the other verbatim.

Headings are argumentative rather than labelling ('Reconfirming — the part people skip', 'What these phrases can't do'), so a skim of headings alone reproduces the article's thesis and escalation sequence.

Four distinct internal destinations, each dropped at the exact point a reader would need the deeper piece (soy sauce → hidden gluten; barley/rye labelling → label guide; trip context → travel guide; venues → /places).

All five FAQ answers trace to body passages (글루텐프리 framing, the one-sentence opener, the no-pronunciation stance, 알러지/알레르기 spelling, and the cross-contamination limits) and each reads standalone as a rich result.
Concrete but thin: the strongest anecdote has a quantity but no venue name or date, and the rest is aggregated pattern ('across a year of asking') rather than dated observed incidents.
criteria.evidence_quote: one bakery owner told us — cheerfully, without being pressed — that his was 10% wheat

criteria.note: Regulatory figures are checkable and the 양조간장/조선간장 distinction is genuinely expert, but romanisation is applied inconsistently (gochujang, doenjang, ssamjang romanised; 간장, 양조간장, 쌀빵 glossed only in English) and not a single product or brand is named.
criteria.evidence_quote: the wheat-free ones advertise it on the label, because for them it's a selling point

criteria.note: The one regulatory claim that carries weight is linked to the primary text on law.go.kr with notice number, issue date, and retrieval date.
A dedicated limits section names what the method cannot establish, refuses to invent a prevalence figure, offers an independent verification path, and carries no commercial or affiliate links.

findings.quote: allergy framing, romanisation, and what to say when the first answer is wrong
findings.why: The description advertises 'romanisation', but the body states outright that it contains none. A searcher clicking for romanised phrases finds the opposite and bounces — a snippet/content mismatch that costs click quality even though the length and keyword rules pass.
findings.fix: Swap 'romanisation' for something the page actually delivers, e.g. 'The Korean phrases that get a kitchen to actually check — allergy framing, copy-ready Hangul, and what to say when the first answer is wrong.'

findings.quote: unless a commercial bottle or tub says otherwise, assume it contains wheat
findings.why: The rule is sound but no product, brand, or label wording is named anywhere in the piece. A reader in a Korean supermarket cannot act on it or verify it, which is the specificity bar for expertise.
findings.fix: Name two or three concrete examples a reader can find on a shelf — e.g. a specific wheat-free 조선간장 or tamari brand you buy, and the exact label phrase that signals it — with the date you last checked the product.

findings.why: Romanisation is applied unevenly: gochujang and doenjang get it, 간장 does not, and later key terms (양조간장, 조선간장, 쌀빵, 밀가루) appear with English glosses only. Inconsistent handling of the same term class weakens the specificity signal and makes terms harder to search for elsewhere.
findings.fix: Pick one convention and hold it — Hangul + romanisation + English on first mention of every term (간장 ganjang / soy sauce; 양조간장 yangjo-ganjang / brewed soy sauce). This is separate from the pronunciation-guide argument, which can stay.

findings.why: This directly contradicts the article's own headline instruction ('Don't try to pronounce it') and FAQ #3 ('Don't — show them instead'). If Google surfaces the FAQ against a page that says the opposite two sections down, the markup and visible content read as inconsistent to a user landing mid-page.
findings.fix: Rewrite to match the show-don't-say stance, e.g. 'Use whichever you copy — either spelling is read the same way.'

findings.quote: during our first year back in Korea (2025–26)
findings.why: The piece's best first-hand moments stay unanchored — the bakery has no name or neighbourhood, the 'year of asking' has no start or end, and no single visit is dated. First-hand signal reads as recalled pattern rather than logged observation.
findings.fix: Anchor two or three episodes: the bakery's district and approximate month, one dated BBQ visit where the grill-plate ask was refused or granted, and one occasion where the reconfirmation caught a wrong first answer.

findings.quote: **양조간장** (brewed soy sauce) is fermented with wheat and is the standard restaurant pour.
findings.why: This is a technical production claim, not an experiential one, yet it carries no citation — unlike the MFDS allergen claim beside it, which is properly sourced and dated. Note only: factual verification is the other judge's axis.
findings.fix: Attach a primary reference for the 양조간장 / 조선간장 distinction (KFDA food type standard or a manufacturer's own ingredient statement) with its publication date, matching the treatment given to 식품등의 표시기준.

criteria.note: Nearly every claim is either sourced (MFDS notice with link and number) or explicitly flagged as the authors' own first-hand pattern; the soy-sauce composition claims are the exception, asserted without any source.
criteria.evidence_quote: (brewed soy sauce) is fermented with wheat and is the standard restaurant pour.

criteria.note: Product categories, the notice number and date, the retrieval date and the anecdote timeframe are all checkable and internally consistent, and the piece explicitly refuses to invent a prevalence figure.

The method (first-hand household experience in Seoul/Gyeonggi, Korean written by a native speaker) and its limits (no sample, no measurement, no lab test, staff turnover, reformulation) are both stated plainly and never dressed up as research.

Framing is otherwise exemplary — coeliac disease is separated from the authors' NCGS, cross-contamination gets its own phrases and its own closing section, and no phrase is sold as making food safe — but one condiment category is declared wheat-free in absolute terms.
criteria.evidence_quote: the meju-based kind used for soups and namul — is soybeans and salt, with no wheat.

criteria.note: The MFDS notice carries its number and issue date, the retrieval month is given, the publication month is stated, and reformulation staleness is explicitly flagged.

Terms, the 알러지/알레르기 distinction, 알레르기 유발물질 and the wheat-only mandatory allergen rule are all correct, but the flagship hand-over card narrows the ask to 밀가루 (wheat flour) where 밀 (wheat) is what soy sauce and barley-adjacent grains actually require.
criteria.evidence_quote: 밀가루, 보리, 호밀 전부 못 먹어요.

criteria.note: The reader is given a primary-source link to the labelling standard, an in-hand ingredient-list method, a phone-ahead route, and an explicit 'How to check independently' section.

findings.quote: 밀가루, 보리, 호밀 전부 못 먹어요.
findings.why: 밀가루 means wheat flour specifically. 양조간장 is brewed with whole wheat (밀), not flour, so a kitchen can honestly answer '밀가루는 안 들어가요' about a soy-based dish while the dish still contains wheat. The body's coeliac table gets this right ('밀, 보리, 호밀 전부 안 돼요'), but the copy-and-hand-over block — the line most readers will actually use — reverts to the narrower word, and the same slip repeats in the following line about 간장.
findings.fix: Change the block to '밀, 보리, 호밀 전부 못 먹어요' and '간장이나 고추장에 밀이 들어가는 경우가 많아서요', keeping 밀가루 only where the opener is deliberately colloquial, and add one clause explaining why the card uses 밀 rather than 밀가루.

findings.quote: the meju-based kind used for soups and namul — is soybeans and salt, with no wheat.
findings.why: This is the only unqualified 'contains no wheat' statement in an otherwise carefully hedged piece. Products sold as 조선간장/한식간장 on Korean shelves are not uniformly meju-only — 혼합간장 blends are common and are not always obvious from the front label — so a coeliac reader could treat the category as a safe default rather than checking the 원재료명.
findings.fix: Qualify to the traditional preparation and add a label check: note that shelf products labelled this way can be 혼합간장 blends, and that the ingredient list still has to be read even inside this category.

findings.quote: (brewed soy sauce) is fermented with wheat and is the standard restaurant pour.
findings.why: The two soy-sauce composition claims are the only factual assertions in the piece carrying neither a source nor an explicit 'this is our observation' marker, and they sit directly under a safety decision a reader makes at a table. Everything else in the article is either linked or attributed, which makes the gap conspicuous.
findings.fix: Either attribute these to the same supermarket-label observation used two paragraphs earlier, or cite the Korean food code's 간장 product-type definitions (식품유형: 양조간장 / 한식간장) so the reader can check the category definitions themselves.
